phases.title: Phase 1 · First Steps
phases.description: Understand what Claude Code is, install it safely, and complete your first small task.

modules.title: What Claude Code is
modules.objective: Understand Claude Code without assuming any terminal or AI coding knowledge.
modules.simple: Claude Code is an AI assistant that works inside a terminal. It can look at files in a project, explain them, suggest changes, edit files, and run commands. You remain in control: you choose the folder, describe the task, review permissions, and check the result.
procedure: Learn three words first: terminal, folder, and command.
Open a terminal and move into a small practice project.
Start Claude Code from that folder.
Ask it to explain the project before changing anything.
Review the result and ask what changed.
modules.bad: Open an important work project and ask Claude to improve everything.
modules.good: Open a disposable practice folder and ask: ‘Explain what is in this folder. Do not change any files.’
modules.exercise: Create a practice folder containing one text file, open Claude Code there, and ask it to explain the file without editing it.
modules.success: You can explain what Claude Code can do, what it cannot safely decide for you, and why the current folder matters.

quiz.question: Who decides which folder and task Claude Code works on?
quiz.explanation: Claude Code works inside the folder you choose and follows the task you provide.

modules.title: How to ask for help clearly
modules.objective: Write simple requests that a first-time user can understand and verify.
modules.simple: A useful request says what you want, what Claude may inspect, what it must not change, and how you will know the task is complete. You do not need technical language. Plain sentences are enough.
procedure: Mention the file, screen, or problem involved.
State any important limit, such as ‘do not delete files.’
Ask Claude to explain its plan before editing when you are unsure.
Ask it to show the changed files and how to test the result.
modules.bad: Fix this.
modules.good: Read README.md and improve spelling and clarity. Do not change commands or technical meaning. Show me the proposed changes before editing.
modules.exercise: Rewrite ‘make my website better’ into a request containing a result, a boundary, and a check.
modules.success: A new user can read the request and understand what should happen and what should remain untouched.

quiz.question: Which request is safest for a beginner?
options: Explain the project first and do not edit files
quiz.explanation: Starting with explanation-only work lets you learn the project before allowing changes.

modules.title: Understand a project before editing it
modules.objective: Learn what a project folder contains using plain-language questions.
modules.simple: A coding project is usually a folder containing source files, configuration files, documentation, and tests. You do not need to understand every file. First ask Claude to identify the important parts and explain them in simple language.
procedure: Ask Claude to list the main folders and important files.
Ask which file starts the application.
Ask how the project is normally run.
Ask for a short beginner-friendly summary.
Do not edit until the map makes sense to you.
modules.bad: Read every file and explain all code at once.
modules.good: Explain this project for a beginner. Show the five most important files, what each one does, and the command used to run the project. Do not edit anything.
modules.exercise: Ask Claude to create a five-item map of a small project and verify that every referenced file exists.
modules.success: You know where the application starts, where its main code lives, and how it can be run or checked.

quiz.question: What should you do before changing an unfamiliar project?
options: Ask for a simple project map
quiz.explanation: A project map gives you context before you approve edits.

modules.title: Make your first safe edit
modules.objective: Complete one small, reversible change from request to verification.
modules.simple: Your first edit should be small and easy to inspect, such as correcting text, changing a heading, or adding a comment. Avoid authentication, payments, deployments, databases, and production systems while learning.
procedure: Choose one small file in a practice project.
Ask Claude to show its plan.
Approve the edit only after the plan is clear.
Open the file and inspect the change.
Run a simple check or ask Claude to explain how to verify it.
Use Git or a backup so the change can be reversed.
modules.bad: Refactor the complete application on my first day.
modules.good: In index.html, change the page heading from ‘Hello’ to ‘Welcome’. Do not modify anything else. After editing, show the exact changed line.
modules.exercise: Change one heading or sentence in a disposable project and verify the old and new text.
modules.success: Only the intended line changed, you inspected it, and you know how to undo it.

quiz.question: What is a good first Claude Code task?
options: Change one heading in a practice file
quiz.explanation: A tiny reversible edit is easy to understand and verify.

phases.title: Phase 2 · Everyday Use
phases.description: Use Claude Code for common coding tasks with clear checks and safe boundaries.

modules.title: Break a large request into small steps
modules.objective: Turn one intimidating task into a sequence of understandable changes.
modules.simple: Large requests are difficult to review. Ask Claude to split the work into small steps where each step produces something you can inspect or test.
procedure: Ask Claude to identify the smallest useful first step.
Review which files that step may change.
Complete and test only that step.
Continue one step at a time.
modules.bad: Build the complete application in one attempt.
modules.good: First show a three-step plan. Implement only step 1: add the empty contact page and a navigation link. Stop before adding the form.
modules.exercise: Split a login feature into page, validation, and server steps.
modules.success: Each step has a visible result and can be reviewed before continuing.

quiz.question: Why use small steps?
options: To make changes easier to review and undo
quiz.explanation: Small steps reduce risk and make mistakes easier to locate.

modules.title: Fix errors without guessing
modules.objective: Give Claude enough evidence to investigate an error safely.
modules.simple: An error message is evidence. Copy the exact message, explain what you were doing, and ask Claude to investigate before changing code. Random edits can hide the real problem.
procedure: Tell Claude the command or action that caused it.
Ask for likely causes and the safest next check.
Make one change at a time.
Run the same action again to confirm the fix.
modules.bad: It does not work. Change whatever is needed.
modules.good: When I run `npm test`, this exact error appears: [paste error]. Explain the likely cause first. Do not edit files until you show the evidence.
modules.exercise: Use a harmless syntax error in a practice project and ask Claude to explain and fix it.
modules.success: The original error no longer occurs, and you understand which change fixed it.

quiz.question: What should you provide when asking Claude to fix an error?
options: The exact error and action that caused it
quiz.explanation: Exact evidence helps Claude investigate instead of guessing.

modules.title: Start, continue, and reset sessions
modules.objective: Understand what Claude remembers inside a session and how to continue safely.
modules.simple: Claude uses the current conversation and project files as working context. Long or unrelated conversations can become confusing. Save a short summary before starting a fresh session.
procedure: Keep one session focused on one task.
Ask for a progress summary before stopping.
Record completed work, changed files, checks, and the next step.
Start a fresh session for unrelated work.
Give the new session the saved summary and ask it to verify the current files.
modules.bad: Use one endless session for many unrelated projects.
modules.good: Create HANDOFF.md with the goal, completed steps, changed files, test result, and next action. Then start a fresh session.
modules.exercise: Write a five-line handoff for a small task.
modules.success: A fresh session can understand the current state without reading the old conversation.

quiz.question: When is a fresh session useful?
quiz.explanation: Fresh sessions reduce confusion from unrelated history.

modules.title: Review and undo changes with Git
modules.objective: Use basic Git checks as a safety net.
modules.simple: Git records file changes. The most useful beginner commands are status and diff: status shows which files changed, and diff shows the changed lines. Commit only after you understand and verify the change.
procedure: Ask Claude to make one focused change.
Commit only the intended files with a clear message.
modules.bad: Commit every changed file without reading the diff.
modules.good: Show `git status` and summarize `git diff`. Identify any unrelated changes before creating a commit.
modules.exercise: Modify one text file, inspect the diff, then restore or commit it.
modules.success: You can see what changed and can return to a known state.

quiz.question: Which command shows changed lines?
quiz.explanation: `git diff` displays the actual line-by-line changes.

modules.title: Understand the safety system around Claude
modules.objective: Recognize that reliable AI work needs more than a good prompt.
modules.simple: Claude works through a surrounding system: your instructions, project files, allowed tools, permissions, tests, Git history, and review. Together these controls make the work safer and more reliable.
procedure: Keep a way to undo changes.
modules.bad: Give Claude broad access and trust it to decide everything.
modules.good: Work in one repository, allow file reads and local tests, review edits, and require approval before push or deployment.
modules.exercise: Write a simple safety checklist for a practice project.
modules.success: You can identify the task boundary, permissions, verification, and rollback method.

quiz.question: What makes Claude Code safer?
quiz.explanation: Reliability comes from controls around the model.

modules.title: Useful everyday commands and habits
modules.objective: Learn only the interface features that remove common beginner friction.
modules.simple: You do not need every shortcut. First learn how to start Claude, stop an action, view help, review permissions, and keep track of the current folder and Git branch.
procedure: Use the built-in help to discover commands.
Learn how to interrupt a running action.
Check the current Git branch before edits.
Add shortcuts only after you understand the manual command.
modules.bad: Install many plugins and aliases before learning the basic workflow.
modules.good: Use the default interface for a week and write down repeated problems before adding one customization.
modules.exercise: Find the help command, current folder, and current Git branch in a practice project.
modules.success: You can identify where Claude is working and stop or inspect its actions.

quiz.question: What should you check before allowing edits?
quiz.explanation: Folder and branch determine where the changes will be made.

phases.title: Phase 3 · Advanced Workflows
phases.description: Introduce reusable instructions, tools, parallel work, permissions, and agent architecture after the basics are comfortable.

modules.title: Use CLAUDE.md for project instructions
modules.objective: Store stable project-specific guidance Claude repeatedly needs.
modules.simple: CLAUDE.md is a project instruction file. Put commands and rules there only when they are stable, important, and not obvious from the project itself.
procedure: Add exact run or test commands.
modules.bad: Fill CLAUDE.md with generic advice and the current conversation.
modules.good: Use `npm test` for checks. Do not edit `src/generated`; run `npm run generate` instead.
modules.exercise: Create a small CLAUDE.md with one command and one project rule.
modules.success: The file is short, accurate, and changes Claude's behavior in a useful way.

quiz.question: What belongs in CLAUDE.md?
quiz.explanation: CLAUDE.md is for durable project guidance.

modules.title: Choose between skills, hooks, MCP, and subagents
modules.objective: Understand each extension mechanism through simple examples.
modules.simple: A skill teaches a reusable method. A hook automatically runs a fixed action at a specific moment. MCP connects Claude to an outside service. A subagent handles a separate focused task with its own context.
procedure: Decide whether it is a method, automatic event, external connection, or separate investigation.
Give it the smallest permissions possible.
modules.bad: Install every extension because it may become useful.
modules.good: Use a hook for formatting, a skill for code review steps, MCP for read-only issue lookup, and a subagent for an isolated security review.
modules.exercise: Match four sample tasks to skill, hook, MCP, or subagent.
modules.success: You can explain why one mechanism is a better fit than the others.

quiz.question: Which mechanism is best for automatically formatting after an edit?
quiz.explanation: Hooks run deterministic actions at defined events.

modules.title: Run independent work in parallel
modules.objective: Use parallel work without creating conflicting edits.
modules.simple: Parallel work helps only when tasks are independent. Two agents should not edit the same files at the same time unless you have a deliberate merge plan.
procedure: Use separate worktrees or branches for writers.
Bring results back to one integration owner.
modules.bad: Ask several agents to rewrite the same module.
modules.good: One agent investigates tests, one reviews security, and one implementation agent edits isolated files; a lead combines the results.
modules.exercise: Mark which parts of a small feature can run in parallel.
modules.success: No two agents unknowingly overwrite the same work.

quiz.question: When is parallel work useful?
quiz.explanation: Independence prevents coordination cost from exceeding the benefit.

modules.title: Design permissions and isolation
modules.objective: Give Claude enough access for the task without exposing unrelated systems.
modules.simple: Permissions control what Claude can reach. Isolation, such as a disposable container or practice repository, limits damage even when a command is wrong.
procedure: List files, tools, network access, and credentials involved.
Allow only what the task needs.
Keep deletion, push, deploy, and external messages explicit.
modules.bad: Disable permission checks on a machine containing important credentials.
modules.good: Run an experiment in a disposable container with only the practice repository mounted and no production secrets.
modules.exercise: Create an allow/ask/deny table for read, test, install, push, and deploy.
modules.success: A mistaken action cannot reach unrelated files, secrets, or production.

quiz.question: What is safer than simply trusting the model?
quiz.explanation: Isolation limits consequences regardless of intent.

modules.title: Separate context, state, and memory
modules.objective: Store information where it remains accurate and useful.
modules.simple: Context is what Claude needs now. State records current progress. Memory stores selected facts useful later. The real source of truth remains the project, database, issue, or document where the fact originates.
procedure: Keep progress in a task file or structured state.
Keep stable rules in project instructions.
Attach a source to important remembered facts.
Load only what the current task needs.
modules.bad: Keep the entire conversation forever and treat it as truth.
modules.good: Store completed task IDs in JSON, project rules in CLAUDE.md, and load only relevant files into a new session.
modules.exercise: Classify ten examples as context, state, memory, or source of truth.
modules.success: A fresh session can resume accurately without the whole old transcript.

quiz.question: Where should current task progress live?
quiz.explanation: Progress changes over time and should be stored as state.

modules.title: Design narrow tools for agents
modules.objective: Create tools that are easy to call, validate, and restrict.
modules.simple: A good tool does one clear job, accepts explicit inputs, returns structured results, and fails with useful errors. Narrow tools are safer than unrestricted shell access.
procedure: Test normal, invalid, and dangerous inputs.
modules.bad: Give the agent a generic shell with production credentials.
modules.good: Provide a read-only operation that accepts a CI run ID and returns the failed job, failed step, log excerpt, and source link.
modules.exercise: Split one broad tool into two smaller operations.
modules.success: Invalid requests fail clearly and unrelated resources remain unreachable.

quiz.question: What is a strong reason to add MCP?
options: A required external capability needs a controlled interface
quiz.explanation: MCP is useful when it provides a needed, permissioned bridge.

modules.title: Coordinate multiple agents
modules.objective: Assign ownership, order, and handoffs across several agents.
modules.simple: Orchestration is work coordination. It defines who owns each task, what must happen first, what output each agent must return, and who verifies the combined result.
procedure: Keep shared decisions with one owner.
modules.bad: Launch many agents on the same vague task.
modules.good: A lead owns architecture; separate agents investigate tests and security; one writer implements; the lead integrates and verifies.
modules.exercise: Create a small dependency diagram for a feature.
modules.success: Every task has one owner, a defined output, and an integration check.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of orchestration?
options: Use as many agents as possible
quiz.explanation: Orchestration manages work and handoffs.

modules.title: Use guardrails and human approval
modules.objective: Reserve human approval for actions with real consequences.
modules.simple: Guardrails prohibit unsafe behavior. Permissions limit available actions. Human gates require a person to approve high-impact steps such as deleting data, pushing code, deploying, purchasing, or sending messages.
procedure: Rate actions by impact and reversibility.
Require approval for external or irreversible actions.
modules.bad: Ask for approval on every file read, or approve every action automatically.
modules.good: Allow local tests automatically, but require approval before push, deploy, deletion, or sending an external message.
modules.exercise: Build a human-approval list for your workflow.
modules.success: Consequential actions cannot happen silently.

quiz.question: Which action clearly needs human approval?
quiz.explanation: Deployment affects an external system and may be difficult to reverse.

modules.title: Measure quality and inspect traces
modules.objective: Know whether an agent succeeded and understand why.
modules.simple: An evaluation checks the result against examples or rules. A trace records what happened: inputs, tool calls, outputs, retries, time, cost, and approvals.
procedure: Track quality, cost, latency, and retries.
modules.bad: It worked once, so it is ready.
modules.good: Run a versioned set of tasks, compare pass rate and cost, and inspect traces for failures before release.
modules.exercise: Create five small evaluation cases for one workflow.
modules.success: A failure can be reproduced and traced to a prompt, tool, data source, or decision.

quiz.question: What does a trace provide?
options: The execution path behind the result
quiz.explanation: Tracing explains how the outcome was produced.

modules.title: Define stopping and recovery rules
modules.objective: Ensure an agent loop cannot continue forever or claim success without proof.
modules.simple: A safe loop has a success check, a maximum number of attempts, time or cost limits, known terminal errors, and a clear path to ask a human for help.
procedure: Set attempt, time, and cost limits.
List errors that should stop immediately.
modules.bad: Keep trying until you feel confident.
modules.good: Stop when tests pass; otherwise stop after three attempts or the budget limit and report the evidence.
modules.exercise: Write success, failure, and escalation exits for one loop.
modules.success: Every run ends as verified success, explicit failure, or human escalation.

quiz.question: What is required besides a success phrase?
quiz.explanation: The model can say it is done incorrectly; external checks and limits are needed.

modules.title: Organize CLAUDE.md for larger projects
modules.objective: Keep instructions relevant by placing them at the correct scope.
modules.simple: Large projects may use a root instruction file plus smaller files for individual areas. General rules belong at the root; frontend-only or backend-only rules should live near those parts.
procedure: Choose global, project, personal, or subsystem scope.
Link detailed references instead of copying everything.
modules.bad: Put all rules, task progress, and directory descriptions in one huge root file.
modules.good: Root file contains commands and shared rules; frontend folder contains UI rules; a handoff file contains current task progress.
modules.exercise: Move four sample rules to the correct scope.
modules.success: Each rule loads only where it is relevant.

quiz.question: Where should frontend-only rules live?
quiz.explanation: Narrow scope reduces irrelevant context.

modules.title: Research, browser, writing, and CI workflows
modules.objective: Use Claude Code beyond editing while preserving sources and verification.
modules.simple: Claude Code can organize research, draft Markdown, inspect CI logs, use browser tools, and prepare artifacts. Keep source links, save outputs in files, and require review before publishing or changing external systems.
procedure: Choose the direct tool for the task.
Use both DOM checks and screenshots for UI.
modules.bad: Research, fix, deploy, and publish everything automatically.
modules.good: Collect cited evidence, create a Markdown draft, diagnose CI, verify changes, and stop at a draft review gate.
modules.exercise: Turn one source into a cited note and an action plan.
modules.success: Claims are sourced, results are saved, and external publication remains reviewed.

quiz.question: What is the safest publishing process?
quiz.explanation: Review separates generation from external action.

phases.title: Phase 4 · Expert Systems
phases.description: Build bounded automation only after the manual workflow is proven and measurable.

modules.title: Automate a proven workflow
modules.objective: Turn a reliable manual process into bounded automation.
modules.simple: Automate only after you understand the normal path, failure cases, inputs, checks, permissions, and recovery. Automation should fail safely and leave evidence.
procedure: Run the process manually several times.
Define inputs, outputs, timeouts, and permissions.
Keep human approval at high-impact boundaries.
modules.bad: Give an unattended agent production access on day one.
modules.good: A CI workflow sends a bounded diff to a read-only reviewer, validates structured findings, and lets a human approve any mutation.
modules.exercise: Add timeout, failure, rollback, and ownership rules to one automation.
modules.success: The automation fails closed, produces logs, and has a named owner.

quiz.question: What should be automated first?
quiz.explanation: A proven process has known inputs, checks, and recovery.

modules.title: Use independent verification
modules.objective: Reduce the chance that the same mistaken assumption survives authoring and review.
modules.simple: A fresh reviewer should compare the change with requirements, inspect callers, run independent checks, and actively search for counterexamples.
procedure: Use a fresh context or reviewer.
Ask for evidence and possible failure cases.
Run independent tests and security checks.
Reconcile findings and document remaining risk.
modules.bad: Ask the authoring session whether its own code is correct.
modules.good: In a fresh session, review the diff against the task, inspect affected callers, run adversarial tests, and report evidence-based findings.
modules.exercise: Design writer, reviewer, and tester roles for one risky change.
modules.success: At least two independent evidence paths support the result.

quiz.question: Why use a fresh reviewer?
quiz.explanation: Fresh context is less attached to the original assumptions.

modules.title: Build your Claude Code operating manual
modules.objective: Keep only practices that repeatedly improve results in your environment.
modules.simple: Record costly failures, useful prompts, checks, rules, skills, and recovery steps. Promote a practice into the manual only after it proves useful more than once.
procedure: Store each lesson in the smallest suitable artifact.
Measure rework, failed checks, acceptance, and cycle time.
Remove tools that add complexity without benefit.
modules.bad: Collect every community tip and plugin.
modules.good: After several similar CI investigations, create a read-only troubleshooting skill and compare its quality for a month.
modules.exercise: Choose one repeated correction and decide where it should live.
modules.success: The system becomes simpler while quality and recovery improve.

quiz.question: What belongs in a long-term manual?
quiz.explanation: Local evidence is more useful than novelty.

modules.title: Ralph loops and long-running builds
modules.objective: Use repeated file-based iterations with hard safety boundaries.
modules.simple: A Ralph loop repeatedly selects one small unfinished story, works on it, runs checks, records progress, and continues. It must use external verification and hard limits rather than trusting a ‘DONE’ message.
procedure: Work on one story per iteration.
Update progress only after checks pass.
Stop on completion, budget, terminal error, or human gate.
modules.bad: Build my whole product overnight and say DONE when finished.
modules.good: In a disposable worktree, implement only the next failing story, run named checks, and stop after 12 iterations or the budget limit.
modules.exercise: Create a three-story task file and a hard-stop policy.
modules.success: False completion cannot end the loop and a bad path cannot run indefinitely.

quiz.question: What makes a Ralph loop trustworthy?
options: Atomic work, external checks, state, and limits
quiz.explanation: Verification and boundaries make repetition useful.

modules.title: Combine hooks, skills, subagents, and MCP
modules.objective: Compose extension mechanisms without overlap or unnecessary authority.
modules.simple: Use project instructions for stable rules, hooks for automatic fixed actions, skills for reusable methods, subagents for isolated reasoning, and MCP for controlled external access.
procedure: Add a second mechanism only when responsibilities remain distinct.
modules.bad: Install a large bundle and repeat the same behavior in every mechanism.
modules.good: A hook blocks secret access, a skill defines security review, a read-only subagent performs it, and MCP retrieves issue context.
modules.exercise: Map five recurring jobs to the smallest mechanism.
modules.success: Each mechanism has one responsibility, owner, and permission boundary.

quiz.question: What should enforce formatting after every edit?
quiz.explanation: Formatting is deterministic event-driven work.

modules.title: Build a sourced knowledge graph
modules.objective: Turn documents into connected notes while preserving provenance and reversibility.
modules.simple: A knowledge graph stores concepts as nodes and relationships as edges. Every useful note and relationship should point back to its source so generated connections can be checked.
procedure: Use an isolated vault or folder.
Create one note per useful concept.
Import into the main system only after audit.
modules.bad: Generate hundreds of unsourced notes directly inside the main vault.
modules.good: Build an isolated folder, preserve source documents, add provenance to each note, sample-check relationships, and import one removable directory.
modules.exercise: Create a five-document mini graph with source backlinks.
modules.success: Every claim is traceable and the import can be removed cleanly.

quiz.question: What prevents unsupported synthesis?
quiz.explanation: Provenance lets each claim be checked against its origin.
